clue.text: Feeling well in France, came running out

indicators.note: out says the jumbled letters sit on the outside, around the French word
running suggests the letters of came are set loose and rearranged

parts.note: bien is French for well

explanation.surface: Someone feeling well in France rushes out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' turns CAME into ACME, split as A M ... C E, and 'out' puts those letters around BIEN to give A M BIEN CE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambience is the mood or atmosphere of a place, the feeling it gives off.

clue.text: Tell, perhaps, of one member of family on air?

definitions.text: one member of family on air?

explanation.surface: A question about whether to tell on a relative broadcasting.
explanation.walkthrough: William Tell is the legendary Swiss crossbowman. The Archers is a long-running BBC radio soap about a farming family, so any of them is one member of a family on air.
explanation.definitionFit: William Tell is the famous Swiss marksman with a bow; a member of the radio soap family shares the surname.

clue.text: British champions in pairs

parts.note: aces are experts or champions at something

explanation.surface: British title-holders competing in doubles events.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is a pair, especially of game birds, so braces are pairs.

clue.text: Team appearing one by one

explanation.surface: A side coming out onto the pitch single file.
explanation.walkthrough: Write the figure one beside another one and it reads 11; a cricket or football side is also called this number.
explanation.definitionFit: A football or cricket side has that many players and is named for the number; two figure ones side by side show the same number.

clue.text: People up here go out with concern

parts.note: to court someone is to go out with them romantically
a concern is a business, as is a house, such as a publishing house

explanation.surface: Someone leaves on a date, anxious about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People up here' means people who are 'up before the judge', on trial in this building.
explanation.definitionFit: Defendants appear, or are 'up', in a building where trials are held.

clue.text: Lamb pieces?

parts.note: not cuts of meat but the writing of Charles Lamb, the English author of the Elia collection

explanation.surface: A butcher's cuts of young sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb was an English writer famous for short prose pieces published under the name Elia.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lamb's best-known works are short literary compositions, the Essays of Elia.

clue.text: Falls for fast fliers

explanation.surface: A tumble that brings down speedy aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: One who swallows a story believes it, falls for it; the birds of that name are quick migrating fliers.

clue.text: Family find some allowances trying

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A family discovers that some pocket money is tiresome.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancestry is family descent, the lineage a genealogist finds when tracing forebears.

clue.text: Bronze tanner short?

parts.note: read as an instruction to brown oneself, the sun being a tanner, perhaps in shorts

explanation.surface: A query about a bronze-coloured sixpence being in short supply.
explanation.walkthrough: A tanner is old British slang for a sixpence coin, but here it is whatever tans the skin; 'bronze' is the verb, to turn brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying in the sunshine to brown the skin is how one acquires a tan.

clue.text: Continental cat taking waters in these bottling premises

parts.note: chat is the French word for cat
eaux is French for waters, Continental carrying over

explanation.surface: A French cat lapping water in a wine cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continental' tells you both words are French.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine estates in Bordeaux, where wine is bottled, are called by the French name for castles.

clue.text: For empty talk, study a boaster

parts.note: gas is idle chatter or hot air
to con is an old word meaning to study or learn

explanation.surface: Learning to swap idle chatter for bragging.
explanation.walkthrough: People from Gascony in France were proverbial braggarts, hence 'gasconade' for boasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Gascony natives had a reputation for bragging, so their name became a byword for a braggart.

clue.text: But should one see the dentist with them?

definitions.text: But should one see the dentist with them?

parts.words: But should one see the dentist with them?
parts.note: teeth that sound as if they are used for seeing, being canines just below the eyes

explanation.surface: A doubt about whether a visit to the dentist is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: The canine teeth of the upper jaw are named after the eyes, so the clue asks whether one sees with them.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper canines are named for lying beneath the eyes.

clue.text: Regrettably unfinished state of large part of America

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Regrettably unfinished state of large part of America', gives ALAS but no word supplies KA; other prints read 'Kay's not finished', so a word (Kay) appears to be missing from the OCR text.
annotationWithheld.clue: Regrettably unfinished state of large part of America

clue.text: Appreciation of strange maid on allotment

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters of maid are made odd, i.e. rearranged

parts.note: a ration is an allotted portion

explanation.surface: A gardener's praise for an odd maid working on her vegetable plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' turns MAID into ADMI; 'on' places RATION after it. An allotment here is not a garden plot but a share.
explanation.definitionFit: Admiration is high regard, an appreciation of someone's merits.

clue.text: Poet giving value to the ordinary things we say

parts.note: words are what we say every day
worth is value

explanation.surface: A poet celebrates everyday speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The value is given 'to' the words, so it follows them.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the English Romantic poet who wrote of using the language of ordinary people.

clue.text: Story-line coarse in construction

indicators.note: construction means the letters are built into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A plot described as crude in the way it is put together.
explanation.definitionFit: A scenario is an outline of the plot of a film or play.

clue.text: Commercial enterprise in river Test, say

parts.note: the Indus is the great river of Pakistan
a test is an example of a trial, a try

explanation.surface: A business on the River Test, a Hampshire trout stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test' looks like part of the river's name (the Test is a river in southern England) but means a trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Industry is manufacturing and trade, commercial activity on a large scale.

clue.text: Calling for this case? Quite the opposite

definitions.text: Calling for this case? Quite the opposite

parts.words: Calling for this case? Quite the opposite
parts.note: not a call for a grammatical case, but the case for calling, the form used to address someone

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a situation demands a summons and is told the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: In Latin grammar, the case used when addressing someone directly is named after calling.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin and other inflected languages, the case for addressing someone takes its name from the Latin for to call.

clue.text: Use of hard pencil before publishing?

definitions.text: Use of hard pencil before publishing?

parts.words: Use of hard pencil before publishing?
parts.note: not drawing with an H pencil but an official firmly striking out text with a blue pencil

explanation.surface: An illustrator's choice of a firm pencil before going to print.
explanation.walkthrough: Censors traditionally struck out passages with a blue pencil; 'hard' means strict, not a grade of lead.
explanation.definitionFit: Suppressing material before print is the job of an official who vets publications.

clue.text: Below motorway, I'm a so twisted plant with drooping leaves

indicators.note: in a down clue, the twisted letters come below, so after, the motorway letter

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

indicators.note: twisted says the letters of I'm a so are rearranged

explanation.surface: A plant wilting beside a motorway, its leaves drooping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twisted' turns IMASO into IMOSA, written under M.
explanation.definitionFit: The sensitive plant of this genus folds and droops its leaves when touched.

clue.text: Empty tin into large tank

indicators.note: into says the tin goes inside the tank

parts.note: a vat is a large vessel for liquids
a can is a tin

explanation.surface: Pouring an empty tin into a large tank.
explanation.definitionFit: A vacant room or seat is empty, unoccupied.

clue.text: Meet cost of iron brought over in cart

indicators.note: in places the turned symbol inside the cart

parts.note: a dray is a low cart for heavy loads, such as beer barrels

indicators.note: brought over in a down clue says the symbol for iron is turned upside down, so read backwards

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: Paying for some iron delivered by cart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought over' reverses FE to EF.
explanation.definitionFit: To defray an expense is to pay or settle it.

clue.text: Aunt go out for chewy sweet?

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of aunt go are put out of order

explanation.surface: An aunt going out to buy a chewy confection.
explanation.definitionFit: Nougat is a chewy confection of sugar, honey and nuts.

clue.text: Chaff not recommended for the elderly

parts.note: something bad is not recommended
in age, i.e. for those of advanced years

explanation.surface: Husks unsuitable for older people's diets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaff' is not husks but teasing banter.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaff as a noun is light-hearted teasing, playful banter.

clue.text: Keep soldiers in check

indicators.note: in places the soldiers inside the check

parts.note: to rein in is to check or restrain
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's reserve soldiers

explanation.surface: Holding troops in restraint.
explanation.definitionFit: To retain is to hold onto or keep.

clue.text: Reptile is around, perhaps? No longer

indicators.note: perhaps hints that is around may be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a reptile is still about and is told it no longer is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' finishes the picture: the reptile is no longer around, being extinct.
explanation.definitionFit: Dinosaurs were prehistoric reptiles, long extinct.

clue.text: Gemstones attached to seductive back

parts.note: on means attached to, as in a button on a coat

indicators.note: back says the word for seductive is read backwards

parts.note: sexy means seductive

explanation.surface: Jewels fixed to an alluring back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns SEXY into YXES.
explanation.definitionFit: Onyx is a banded variety of chalcedony used as a semi-precious stone.

clue.text: Soldiers taking tot before going to the line

parts.note: a tot is a small child, an infant
RY stands for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Troops taking a child along before heading to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the line' looks like the front line but is a railway line, abbreviated RY.
explanation.definitionFit: The infantry are foot soldiers.
